meta.title: F2 numbers: the stock-and-flow presets, the two feedback loops and the whole-system map
meta.note: Every number in the three stock-and-flow presets is illustrative and comes from the model in f02-systems-and-map.js with the parameters below. The battery is Prairie Town's battery from lesson 9 (25 MW, 100 MWh, 80% round trip, the whole loss taken on charging). The ripple map shows first-round directions of change, other things equal, for a grid like the Plains Grid; it is a thinking tool, not a model, and states no sizes. Its waves are steps in tracing causes, not fixed delays: each wave's label says roughly when that step plays out, and effects that happen together share a wave. Operating responses (which plants run, prices, emissions) come in the first waves; bills and investment, which follow tariffs and planning, come later. Where an outcome depends on a condition (what replaces gas, the tariff, what serves a new load), the reason says so. Each preset's `about` is a list of short labeled rows (setup, units, rule). Real-world numbers carry their source and date under `sources`.

reservoir.label: Reservoir

about.t: Illustrative: a hydro reservoir upstream on the Plains Grid, fed by a river that swells with spring snowmelt.
Water counts as the electricity it can make (GWh). Flows are average MW over one week of 168 hours.
Change in the stock each week, in GWh = (river in − release, in MW) × 168 ÷ 1,000.

inflow.formula: MW in week w (w = 0 … 51) = base + amp × exp(−((w − peak) ÷ width)²)

reservoir.task: Choose a steady release for the turbines. Get through the year without spilling water and without running dry.

battery.label: Battery

about.t: Prairie Town's battery from lesson 9 (illustrative): 25 MW, 100 MWh; it gives back 80% of the electricity bought to charge it.
The whole loss is taken on charging. It charges from 10:00 to 15:00, discharges from 18:00 to 22:00, and starts the day empty.

battery.task: Deliver as much energy as the battery can hold in the evening, without asking it for energy it does not have.

carbon.label: Carbon budget

about.t: Illustrative: a nation emits 100 Mt of CO₂ in 2025 (Mt = million tonnes) and allows itself 1,500 Mt in all from 2025 on.
Emissions change in straight lines: to the 2035 level, then to zero in the net-zero year, or they stay at the 2035 level.
The counter adds up CO₂ emitted since the start of 2025. It does not model how much of it stays in the air.

predict.q: The nation halves its emissions by 2035, then holds them there. After 2035, the CO₂ it has emitted since 2025 (the stock)…

carbon.task: Choose the 2035 level and the net-zero year. Keep the nation's cumulative CO₂ within its budget to 2070.

ev.label: Chargers and EVs
ev.lede: Do more electric cars bring more public chargers, and more chargers more cars?

links.why: More EVs on the road use public chargers more.
More use makes new chargers pay, so more get built.
More chargers make owning an EV easier.
Sales add to the EVs on the road, a stock.
More EVs mean longer queues at the chargers that exist.
Longer queues make owning an EV less convenient.

loops.why: More EVs bring more chargers, which bring more EVs, and it can run backwards too: fewer EVs, fewer chargers.
Growth lengthens the queues, and the queues slow the growth.

rebound.label: The rebound effect
rebound.lede: A home swaps old bulbs for LEDs. Does it save all the energy the engineers expected?

links.why: Better bulbs give the same light with less energy.
Cheaper light gets used more: brighter rooms, lights left on.
More hours of light use more energy.
More energy used means less of the expected saving is kept.

loops.why: Part of the saving is spent on more light, so the saving shrinks but does not vanish.

nodes.label: Electricity demand
nodes.def: How much power homes and businesses draw, hour by hour (MW).

nodes.label: Which plants run
nodes.def: The plants an operator calls on each hour, usually cheapest first: the [[merit-order|merit order]].

nodes.label: Wires and connections
nodes.def: The lines and substations that carry power, and the links that connect new loads and plants.

nodes.label: What gets built
nodes.def: New plants, storage, lines and efficiency that owners and planners choose to invest in.

nodes.label: Wholesale price
nodes.def: The [[wholesale-price|wholesale price]]: what power plants are paid for each MWh in the market.

nodes.label: Household bills
nodes.def: What homes pay for electricity and heat under their [[tariff|tariff]].

nodes.label: Gas import bill
nodes.def: What a region pays others for the gas it buys from them.

nodes.label: Grid upgrade costs
nodes.def: The cost of new lines and substations, which some group of customers or owners pays.

nodes.label: CO₂ emissions
nodes.def: CO₂ from burning fuels in power plants and homes, in tonnes a year.

nodes.label: Local air pollution
nodes.def: Smoke, soot and other pollutants in the air near plants that burn fuel.

nodes.label: Water use
nodes.def: The water that power plants and cooling systems draw from rivers, lakes or the ground.

nodes.label: Energy burden
nodes.def: The [[energy-burden|energy burden]]: the share of a household's income spent on energy.

nodes.label: Jobs and tax base
nodes.def: Work building and running energy plants, and the local taxes they pay.

nodes.label: Heat-related health risk
nodes.def: The risk of illness or death from extreme heat, highest for people without cooling.

nodes.label: Spare capacity
nodes.def: How much more the available plants and lines could supply than demand needs right now: the grid's cushion.

nodes.label: Dependence on imported gas
nodes.def: How much of a region's energy relies on gas brought in from elsewhere.

levers.label: Gas price doubles

predict.q: Before the ripple: what happens to CO₂ emissions?

levers.note: This is an adaptation chain, not a feedback loop: over time, switching away from gas can reduce exposure to future gas-price shocks.

effects.why: Where gas plants set the price in many hours, the wholesale price climbs with their fuel cost (lesson 8).
A region that imports gas pays more for the same fuel.
Plants that burn other fuels, where they exist, run more in the next hours' dispatch; gas plants run less.
If coal plants fill in, CO₂ rises; if no other plant can take over, gas keeps running and little changes.
Homes heated with gas pay more for heat once their tariff passes the price on.
Low-income homes spend a larger share of their income on energy, so higher bills weigh on them most.
Efficiency, wind, solar, storage and other fuels become more attractive to build.
As the system switches away from gas, it depends less on imported gas.

predict.q: Before the ripple: what happens to spare capacity?

effects.why: Air conditioning pushes demand toward its peak.
Hot lines sag and can carry less: their ratings fall as the air warms (DOE).
Demand is up while hot lines and some thermal plants (plants that make electricity from heat) deliver less, so spare capacity shrinks from both sides (NERC).
People without cooling face more risk to their health.
[[peaker|Peakers]], plants used mainly in the hours of highest demand, and power from neighboring grids fill the gap.
Tight hours can bring [[scarcity-price|scarcity prices]].
In a grid like Prairie Town's, the extra MWh come from gas peakers (lesson 0).
Higher costs can reach bills later; how much depends on the tariff.
Low-income homes feel higher bills and cooling costs most.
Repeated tight hours can encourage planners to add capacity, demand response, storage or stronger lines.

predict.q: Before the ripple: assume demand stays the same and gas plants with spare capacity can replace coal. What happens to CO₂ emissions?
predict.cond: if gas plants with spare capacity can replace coal

waves.label: Hours to days, once the price applies

effects.why: Coal's running cost rises more than gas's, since it emits more CO₂ per MWh, so gas plants can move ahead of coal plants in the [[merit-order|merit order]].
When a fossil plant sets the price, the price now includes its carbon cost.
If gas plants with spare capacity replace coal, CO₂ per MWh falls.
If less coal is burned, local air pollution falls too.
If the tariff passes the higher wholesale price on, power bills rise.
It depends on the revenue: returned to households as rebates, it can offset the burden.
Low-carbon plants and efficiency become more attractive to build.
Jobs shift: fewer at coal mines and plants, as in Ridge County; more where new plants are built.
If old plants retire before new ones connect, spare capacity shrinks; planners manage the sequence.

levers.label: A new data center

predict.q: Before the ripple: what happens to CO₂ emissions?

levers.about: A 300 MW data-center campus, an illustrative large load that runs around the clock.

effects.why: A 300 MW load running around the clock adds demand in every hour.
It needs new lines or a substation before it can draw its full power.
With supply unchanged, the new load uses up spare capacity as soon as it connects.
Construction can bring jobs, and the site a larger local tax base.
Cooling may draw water, depending on the cooling design.

waves.label: From its first hours of running

effects.why: Existing plants run more hours to serve the extra MWh.
Prices can rise in tight hours.
It depends on which plants serve the extra MWh: up if fossil plants fill in, less if new low-carbon supply is added.
Someone pays for the new lines and substations.
Whether other customers' bills rise depends on who pays for upgrades under the tariff: Analyst lesson [[lesson:a04-retail-tariffs|A4]].
Developers and planners may add new supply and lines.

ipcc_tcre.what: Each 1,000 Gt of cumulative CO₂ emissions is assessed to likely cause 0.27 °C to 0.63 °C of warming, best estimate 0.45 °C; reaching net zero CO₂ is required to stabilize human-induced warming.
ipcc_tcre.source: IPCC (2021), Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis, Summary for Policymakers, D.1.1, p. 28

sorrell_rebound.what: For household energy services in the OECD, the paper concludes that the direct rebound effect should generally be less than 30% (abstract; the full text is not openly readable).
sorrell_rebound.source: Sorrell, Dimitropoulos and Sommerville (2009), Empirical estimates of the direct rebound effect: a review, Energy Policy 37(4), 1356-1371

li_ev.what: From quarterly EV sales and charging-station deployment in 353 U.S. metro areas, 2011-2013, the empirical analysis finds indirect network effects on both sides of the market, stronger on the EV demand side; the paper's model shows such effects form feedback loops (abstract).
li_ev.source: Li, Tong, Xing and Zhou (2017), The market for electric vehicles: indirect network effects and policy design, Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists 4(1), 89-133

bathtub.what: Subjects from an elite business school with essentially no prior exposure to system dynamics showed a poor understanding of stock and flow relationships and time delays (abstract; the full text is not openly readable).
bathtub.source: Booth Sweeney and Sterman (2000), Bathtub dynamics: initial results of a systems thinking inventory, System Dynamics Review 16(4), 249-286

nerc_sra.what: NERC's summer assessment counts derates of thermal plants in extreme heat among the risks to supply; in one U.S. region they could take about 3 GW from available supply.
nerc_sra.source: NERC (May 2025), 2025 Summer Reliability Assessment, Table 3, p. 14

doe_dlr.what: A line's thermal limit depends on the air temperature, wind speed and sunshine; conductors sag as they heat up.
doe_dlr.source: U.S. DOE (June 2019), Dynamic Line Rating, Report to Congress, p. 11

eia_peak.what: Hot weather, with an underlying rise in demand, pushed Lower 48 coincident peak demand to a record 759,180 MW on 29 July 2025.
eia_peak.source: EIA, Today in Energy: U.S. electricity peak demand set new records twice in July

doe_dc.what: Data centers consumed about 4.4% of total U.S. electricity in 2023 (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's report).
doe_dc.source: U.S. DOE, DOE Releases New Report Evaluating Increase in Electricity Demand from Data Centers
